title: Lateral Field Bleed: Protocols and Priority Targets — Executable Methods for Inverted Fan Construction, Symbolon Design, and Disciplinary Bridge Packet Series (v3.1)
creator: Lee Sharks
description:
Lateral Field Bleed v3.1 defines how an archive concept may begin appearing in adjacent AI-search questions that do not name it directly. The doctrinal correction is crucial: the protocol’s preferred use is not to privatize broad disciplinary terms but to create transparent bridge packets where the archive offers a substantial clarification, extension, or taxonomy. Direct retrieval stabilizes a node; lateral bleed concerns the edges that make the node relevant to neighboring fields.

The protocol separates documented mechanisms, inferred mechanisms, and engineered targets. It describes query fan-out, retrieval candidate selection, dense-vector adjacency, citation/composition divergence, GraphRAG as a modeling lens, institutional regeneration, temporal phases, scoring, query coordinates, inverted fans, symbolons, aphoristic “teeth,” and provenance membranes. It also states that a concept cannot be summoned from nowhere and that production search systems should not be presumed to use web-scale GraphRAG. The document is a research and publication-design protocol; it should not be represented as covert control over rankings or proof that querying and deposition cause the claimed system behavior.

wiki_article:
**Lateral Field Bleed** is an archive protocol by Lee Sharks for studying and designing concept propagation across adjacent AI-search fields.

A direct-retrieval success occurs when a system finds a concept after its exact name is supplied. Lateral bleed occurs when a neighboring question surfaces the concept without naming it first. Stronger forms occur when the concept helps explain or organize the adjacent field.

Version 3.1 corrects an earlier proprietary emphasis. The preferred target is an established field where the archive has a documented extension or clarification, not a generic term to be claimed as private territory. Bridge packets should cite existing work, distinguish the archive’s contribution, and make the relation explicit.

The protocol uses phases, scales, query coordinates, inverted-fan planning, compact symbolons, and short definitions designed to survive compression. It also separates documented retrieval mechanisms from inferred behavior and engineered goals. Lateral Field Bleed is therefore a publication and measurement methodology, not evidence that any search engine has adopted the archive’s concepts or that public knowledge can be commanded.
